methods.title: Recall before you reveal
methods.principle: Producing an answer from memory is a learning activity, not only a way to measure knowledge. Experiments found that repeated retrieval supported delayed retention better than repeatedly studying the same material without retrieval.
methods.implementation: Show the card prompt first. Ask the student to say or write a complete answer before revealing it, then compare the attempted answer with the explanation. Keep successfully recalled cards in later reviews.
methods.limits: The cited experiments were not CLAT trials. A correct card response does not establish legal understanding or predict an exam score.

methods.title: Return after a gap
methods.principle: Revisiting material on different occasions can improve later retention. The useful gap depends on how long the learner needs to retain the material; one interval is not best for every deadline.
methods.implementation: Schedule cards across days, with due reviews before optional new cards. An easy-to-understand 1/3/7-day progression is a product heuristic; a forgotten card returns sooner. Never schedule a necessary final review after the exam.
methods.limits: The cited fact-learning study does not validate this site's exact intervals, ratings or legal-content scheduler.

methods.title: Repair the answer, including lucky guesses
methods.principle: Feedback can support learning after errors and after answers that are correct but uncertain. In two general-knowledge experiments, confirming low-confidence correct responses helped their later retention.
methods.implementation: After every quiz attempt, show the correct option and a reasoned explanation with its source. Offer uncertain correct answers as well as errors for the repair queue; ask what made the nearest distractor wrong.
methods.limits: Immediate feedback is used here for convenient study flow, not claimed to be the optimal timing in every learning situation.

methods.title: Learn a distinction, then mix it
methods.principle: Mixed practice can make learners choose which approach fits instead of assuming every item uses the last rule studied. A mathematics experiment found better delayed performance after mixed rather than blocked problem types.
methods.implementation: Introduce a topic with its lesson and a few focused questions. Then mix previously studied topics and contrast close alternatives, such as admissibility versus weight or contractual remedies versus tort liability.
methods.limits: The cited result concerns mathematics. Transfer to CLAT law preparation is a reasoned design choice, not a demonstrated effect or a reason to mix unfamiliar material indiscriminately.

methods.title: Explain why the rule fits
methods.principle: Explaining the steps of a worked example can connect its solution to underlying principles. In a small mechanics study, stronger learners generated more useful explanations and monitored gaps in their understanding more accurately.
methods.implementation: Before reading a worked answer, complete: issue, applicable rule, decisive fact, exception, and conclusion. Then change one fact and explain whether the conclusion should change. Check the explanation against the supplied material.
methods.limits: The cited study is small and observational; it does not prove this exact legal template causes higher exam marks. Explanations still need reliable corrective feedback.

methods.title: Separate familiarity from knowledge
methods.principle: Seeing an answer while studying can create a misleading feeling of competence. Research on paired associates found that judgments made with both cue and answer visible did not simply mirror later recall from the cue alone.
methods.implementation: Record confidence before revealing a card or submitting an answer. Review confidence alongside accuracy, especially confident errors. Use later unseen attempts to judge improvement rather than completion counts alone.
methods.limits: Confidence is not a calibrated probability by default. A small set of repeated questions cannot establish a student's true exam accuracy or readiness.

scheduleAdvice.status: editorial template, not a tested optimum
scheduleAdvice.final72Hours: Prioritise due cards, recurring personal errors and short mixed practice. Avoid filling the final days with unreviewable new material. Keep a sensible stopping time and prepare exam logistics.
scheduleAdvice.adaptation: Reduce new material first when time is short. Do not remove feedback or let a large due queue silently crowd out passage practice. No minimum daily time or full-deck completion is guaranteed to produce a particular score.
